research_text:
## Research brief

### 1. Governed API and the reported event/value

`javax.net.ssl.SSLContext` represents a secure-socket protocol implementation and serves as a factory for secure socket factories and `SSLEngine` instances. It is initialized with key managers, trust managers, and a source of secure random bytes.  
Source: https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/javax/net/ssl/SSLContext.html ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/javax/net/ssl/SSLContext.html))

The detector message refers specifically to the second argument, `tm`, of:

```text
SSLContext.init(KeyManager[] km, TrustManager[] tm, SecureRandom random)
```

The documented value is `tm == null`. The Java API explicitly permits this: when either manager-array argument is `null`, installed security providers are searched for the highest-priority implementation of the appropriate factory; for `tm`, that is the appropriate trust-manager factory. The JSSE guide says the result is an appropriate `TrustManager` obtained from the highest-priority `TrustManagerFactory`. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/javax/net/ssl/SSLContext.html))

Thus, the detector phrase “platform default trust managers” is a summary of provider-selected behavior. The API’s own wording is more precise: it performs a provider search for the highest-priority appropriate factory. It is not an API error to pass `null`. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/javax/net/ssl/SSLContext.html))

A `TrustManager` makes the peer-authentication trust decision; the JSSE guide states that if presented credentials are not trusted, the connection is terminated. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/11/security/java-secure-socket-extension-jsse-reference-guide.html))

**Rule-label caveat:** In the supplied CrySL source, the null-`tm` issue corresponds textually to the `REQUIRES generatedTrustManagers[tm];` predicate, not to its `CONSTRAINTS` section, which constrains only `protocol`. The source does not define how a particular detector version maps this to the presentation label `UnsatisfiedConstraint`; that label cannot be resolved from the rule file alone. ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/SSLContext.crysl))

---

### 2. Officially documented usage and remediation guidance

#### Documented valid usage

The Java API documents these valid alternatives for trust managers:

* Pass `null` for `tm`, allowing provider-selected trust-manager-factory behavior.
* Supply one or more `TrustManager` objects explicitly.
* Obtain trust managers from a `TrustManagerFactory`.
* Supply a concrete trust-manager implementation; the JSSE guide specifically notes that a factory is not required when an application implements `X509TrustManager`. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/javax/net/ssl/SSLContext.html))

`TrustManagerFactory` is documented as a factory for trust managers based on trust material from a `KeyStore` and/or provider-specific sources. Its `init(KeyStore)` and `init(ManagerFactoryParameters)` methods are the documented initialization mechanisms, and its `getTrustManagers()` method returns the managers it produces.  
Source: https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/javax/net/ssl/TrustManagerFactory.html ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/javax/net/ssl/TrustManagerFactory.html))

#### What the official sources recommend when explicit selection is needed

The official sources do **not** characterize `init(..., null, ...)` as incorrect or unsafe, and they do **not** prescribe replacing it as a general remediation. It is expressly API-valid. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/javax/net/ssl/SSLContext.html))

Where an application needs explicit trust-manager selection or provider-specific trust-material configuration, the JSSE guide documents the supported approach: initialize a suitable `TrustManagerFactory` with the appropriate `KeyStore` or provider-specific `ManagerFactoryParameters`, then use the factory-produced managers when initializing `SSLContext`. The guide presents this as a supported usage pattern, not as a mandatory migration from `null`. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/11/security/java-secure-socket-extension-jsse-reference-guide.html))

The sources do not establish that merely changing provenance from provider-selected managers to factory-returned managers preserves the same trust material, provider choice, revocation configuration, or validation behavior. Those depend on the selected provider, factory algorithm, and factory initialization inputs. In particular, the documented default factory algorithm is configurable through the `ssl.TrustManagerFactory.algorithm` security property. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/javax/net/ssl/TrustManagerFactory.html))

No conclusion about hostname-verification behavior follows from this `SSLContext.init` documentation alone.

#### Protocol-name distinction

The JCA standard names distinguish `"TLS"`, `"TLSv1.2"`, and `"TLSv1.3"`: `"TLS"` supports some version of TLS and may support other SSL/TLS versions; a version-specific name supports that version and may also support others. Separately, the JSSE guide says that enabled protocols are controlled on the created `SSLSocket`, `SSLServerSocket`, or `SSLEngine` through `setEnabledProtocols`. Therefore, a requested `SSLContext` algorithm name alone is not documentation of the enabled or negotiated protocol. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/specs/security/standard-names.html))

---

### 3. Compatibility, formats, platform support, and migration

* **Persisted formats:** The reviewed `SSLContext` and `TrustManagerFactory` API documentation specifies no persisted configuration format and no persistence-format compatibility commitment for replacing a null `TrustManager[]` with an explicit array. The JSSE guide does document SSL session state as associated with a context and reusable by objects created under that context, but it does not specify a persisted session format or migration process for this change. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/11/security/java-secure-socket-extension-jsse-reference-guide.html))

* **Wire formats:** The reviewed sources do not state that the `TrustManager[]` parameter itself has a TLS wire representation, nor do they provide a wire-format migration procedure for changing this argument. The sources define trust managers in terms of local peer-authentication trust decisions. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/11/security/java-secure-socket-extension-jsse-reference-guide.html))

* **API-version support:** `SSLContext` and `TrustManagerFactory` have both existed since Java 1.4. The null-manager behavior is documented in Java SE 8 and current Java documentation, so use of factory-created `TrustManager[]` does not introduce a newer API surface than these classes and methods. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/javase/8/docs/api/javax/net/ssl/SSLContext.html))

* **Protocol-version support:** Current Java SE documentation requires platform implementations to support `TLSv1.2` and `TLSv1.3`. In contrast, the Java SE 8 API documentation listed only `TLSv1` as the required standard `SSLContext` protocol and directed users to implementation release documentation for additional support. A move to version-specific `TLSv1.2` or `TLSv1.3` therefore requires confirmation against the actual target JDK/provider set; this cannot be inferred merely from the presence of `SSLContext`. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/javax/net/ssl/SSLContext.html))

* **Documented migration path:** No official migration procedure was found for replacing `tm == null` with factory-generated trust managers. The official documentation provides supported APIs and examples, but not an equivalence guarantee or a compatibility recipe.

---

### 4. Exact CrySL rule scope, method patterns, parameter constraints, and conditions

Primary rule source:  
https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/SSLContext.crysl ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/SSLContext.crysl))

The rule declares the governed specification type as `javax.net.ssl.SSLContext`. Its verbatim scope and event clauses are:

```text
SPEC javax.net.ssl.SSLContext

FORBIDDEN
	getDefault() => Get;

EVENTS
	g1: getInstance(protocol);
	g2: getInstance(protocol, _);
	Get := g1 | g2;

	i1: init(km, tm, random);
	Init := i1;

	se1: eng = createSSLEngine();
	se2: eng = createSSLEngine(_,_);
	Engine := se1 | se2;
```

([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/SSLContext.crysl))

The source also declares the event variables as:

```text
java.lang.String protocol;
javax.net.ssl.KeyManager[] km;
javax.net.ssl.TrustManager[] tm;
javax.net.ssl.SSLEngine eng;
java.security.SecureRandom random;
```

([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/SSLContext.crysl))

Accordingly, as written:

| Event | Method name and parameter-list constraint in the rule |
|---|---|
| Forbidden event | `getDefault()` — zero parameters; mapped to `Get` with `=> Get` |
| `g1` / `Get` | `getInstance(protocol)` — one declared `java.lang.String` variable |
| `g2` / `Get` | `getInstance(protocol, _)` — two arguments; the second is wildcarded |
| `i1` / `Init` | `init(km, tm, random)` — three declared variables: `KeyManager[]`, `TrustManager[]`, `SecureRandom` |
| `se1` / `Engine` | `eng = createSSLEngine()` — zero parameters |
| `se2` / `Engine` | `eng = createSSLEngine(_, _)` — two wildcarded parameters |

The rule’s remaining verbatim conditions are:

```text
ORDER
	Get, Init, Engine?
CONSTRAINTS
	protocol in {"TLSv1.2", "TLSv1.3"};

REQUIRES
	generatedKeyManagers[km];
	generatedTrustManagers[tm];
	randomized[random];

ENSURES
	generatedSSLContext[this] after Init;
	generatedSSLEngine[eng] after Engine;
```

([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/SSLContext.crysl))

**Receiver type / same-name methods:** No—the rule is scoped by its declaration `SPEC javax.net.ssl.SSLContext`; it does not declare a global, name-only matcher for arbitrary methods named `init`, `getInstance`, `getDefault`, or `createSSLEngine`. The raw rule source contains no alternate receiver type or text authorizing matching a method solely because it shares one of those names. However, the source file itself does not define CrySL tool dispatch, inheritance, overload-resolution, or analysis-resolution semantics; resolving those implementation details would require separate CrySL-language and detector-version documentation.

**Source limitation:** The supplied rule URL points to a mutable `master` branch. This brief reports the rule text retrieved from that URL; it does not independently verify the supplied SHA-256 value against a fixed repository commit or compiled rule artifact.
